title: Electric Current
summary: Electric current is the flow of electric charge through a wire — billions of electrons walking past each second, measured in amps. In this model a glowing wire carries a streaming tennis-ball-belt of electrons between a battery and a bulb; slow down, speed up, and watch the ammeter and brightness move together.

plainLanguageExplanation: Electric current is the flow of charge down a wire — trillions of electrons shuffling together, like water through a pipe. We measure it in amperes (A): one amp is a coulomb of charge passing a point each second. Water analogies make it simple: the electron stream is the water, the wire is the pipe, and the battery is the pump. In this model a transparent wire shows the electron flow as a stream of dots, and a slider tunes the flow — high ammeter, fast stream, bright bulb. Key truths: current happens only when the loop is complete (a broken wire stops the flow), and the whole loop shares the same current — fewer electrons at any point would mean fewer everywhere. Amps are the how-much-moves number you'll see on charger labels, fuse ratings, and power strips; the bigger the amps, the brighter the bulb and the thicker the dose of electrons to the device.

whyItMatters: Current is the volume knob of electricity: how much charge the 'pipe' delivers decides heat, light, and power in every wire. Appliances name their current draw on the label; fuses and breakers exist to cut off dangerous current; battery ratings are built on amps. 'Amps' is the practical face of electricity everyone touches.
didYouKnow: A single gram of copper wire contains more free electrons than there are seconds in the history of the universe — currents are trillions upon trillions of charges marching together. Yet electrons drift at just centimeters per hour; the push passes nearly at light speed.
compareReason: Current is how much charge flows; voltage is how hard it is pushed. The dot rail keeps the same pipe but its reservoir height changes the flow — two knobs, one loop.
